CS2 right now is basically a simulator of playing against $5 cheater accounts.

Every second Premier match and almost every regular MM game turns into a circus. You put in thousands of hours learning nades and grinding aim, and the guy on the other team has an empty profile, 2 hours played and prefires through smokes. Or he’s a “smurf” who’s “just having a good day”. For the fifth time tonight.

Banning single accounts does nothing. These guys keep 5-10 accounts at once, buy Prime, drop some cheap skins on them so the profile looks legit, and just hop to the next one when the old one gets hit. Report all you want, a fresh account costs less than a coffee.

Mid and high rating Premier is its own kind of hell. Spinbots, aimlock, barely even hidden. From what I see in my games, VAC Live catches basically nothing in real time.

And then the “solution” everyone gives you is: just go play FACEIT. So to get a normal game in a game I already own, I have to install third party software with a kernel driver that loads every time my PC boots, turn on Secure Boot and TPM 2.0, and it only works on Windows 10/11. https://support.faceit.com/hc/en-us/articles/9394666828188
Why is that my problem? Why does a separate company, which isn’t even Valve (it’s owned by a Saudi state-backed group), have to do the job Valve should be doing on its own servers? Valve is fine with this setup because FACEIT does the dirty work and they don’t have to spend a cent. Honestly sometimes it looks like Gabe just doesn’t want to see it.

The funniest part is that regular players are doing Valve’s job for free. A guy from NTNU in Norway wrote his master’s thesis on making bans follow the person, not the account. His system looks at demos and recognizes a player by how they move the mouse and press keys. On 1000+ players it almost always picked the right person and even found smurfs nobody knew about.
https://www.pcgamer.com/hardware/counter-strike-2-player-dedicates-masters-thesis-to-rooting-out-cheaters-creates-grade-a-player-tracking-system/
Another guy built an open source server-side anticheat for community servers, CS2AC, with 17 detection modules: aim, silent aim, bhop and more. One person.
https://github.com/karola3vax/CS2AC
And a billion dollar company apparently can’t.

So players are writing theses and anticheats, and Valve is releasing another case.

Don’t buy skins and don’t open cases until they actually fix anticheat. Money is the only thing they notice.

Apex Legends used to be an incredible game—especially around 2020 and the years that followed. The movement, the gunplay, the characters, the pacing… it all came together in a way that made it one of the most exciting battle royales out there. It was even the game that kicked off my streaming journey, so I’ll always have a soft spot for it.

But somewhere along the way, the magic faded. Instead of focusing on long‑standing bugs or quality‑of‑life fixes, the developers kept pumping out new content, reworking characters that didn’t need to be touched, and releasing new legends that felt overpowered right out of the gate. The balance issues piled up, and the game slowly shifted from fun and competitive to sweaty and exhausting.

These days, the lobbies feel dominated by players who treat every match like a tournament, and that casual, chaotic fun the game used to have just isn’t there anymore. The core of what made Apex special is buried under layers of imbalance and design choices that never quite landed.

I’ll always appreciate what the game meant to me, but it doesn’t feel the same—and at this point, it probably never will.

Respawn is not the same company that made Titanfall 2 anymore. This is published by EA so you know there's no real progression unless you spend ungodly amounts of money for skins that don't look good. You would think for a game with such good movement, EA would realize how good this game could be. Unfortunately the pros in this game aren't good enough to move to another game, and any new players immediately leave because this game also lags like crazy. There is literally no reason to play this game. I have played it since launch, and it's not like it's gotten a 2.0 or health update to the game. I'm begging you, please just don't play this game. But if you do, add me I guess.

Preface: I do recommend this game - Only for short lengths of time. Maybe an hour or two TOPS. Any more than that and you run the risk of rage quitting and uninstalling due to one or more of the issues I list below. You have been warned.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

This game has now been around for over 2 years. PLENTY of time for the developers to establish a trusting relationship with their players/users. Typically, that is what a decent developer does: A swath of players will complain about a certain aspect of the game and the developers will actually listen and at least make attempts at fixing the problems.

NOT. IN. THIS. CASE. EVER.

I understand that a portion of what a game developing company does is supposed to generate revenue for the company - And they do! A separate, and equally important, aspect is that the company is also supposed to improve the game by listening to their users and addressing issues in a timely manner - hopefully, before their users get angry enough to drop the game altogether.

This is precisely where EA/Respawn have failed. And I will break it down for you, precisely HOW they have failed.

1. Cheaters:
This game has an inordinate amount of cheaters. There really is no easy way to say it. And it is OBVIOUS and BLATANT. EA relies upon the absolutely defunct Easy Anti-Cheat system. Please, hold your laughter... In their defense, however, they have made sure to spread rumors of a revamped anti-cheat system, designed specifically for Apex. The real issue is how LONG they have been spreading this rumor. I can only assume that it was a PR stunt to quiet those complaints of cheaters. How can I make that assumption? Mainly because they seem to focus on things of little or no consequence - Like adding badges to shield batteries and medkits... I mean, what?! Why would you focus on cosmetics when you have a huge cheater problem?!

2. Match-Making (MM):
Very rarely have I seen an MM quite as laughable as the one being used in Apex. I understand that there it a lot of complexity involved, what with ranked splits resetting every month (for the most part) and making everyone, essentially, noobs. But, there is a SUPER easy way to fix it (which I will detail later). I understand why they do the ranked split as well: they want to force players to play more often to keep their ranking high - DUH! The more players there are, the more likely it is that they make money and that those players will spread the word so that even more players will play and give them even more opportunity to make more money. But an MM based solely on your current in-game rank is absolutely asinine. And that is just ranked. What if you don't play ranked? Good luck! You could be paired against ANYONE, professional players and noobs alike.

3. Maps:
Currently, there are a total of five maps in Apex (for BR). Every season they have two maps in rotation for pub games. TWO. And those two maps rotate every hour or so. For ranked matches, they use ONE. Over and over, on and on... Maps should be randomized except in tournaments. Going into a game, you should not know where you are going to land, what characters you should be playing, etc. It should be a friggin' BATTLE ROYALE! Formulate your plan based on who is on your team and what the map is, ad-hoc, just like everyone else. No one should know what map your're landing on until the drop ship starts its flight across it. Add some aspect mystery to the game.

4. Weapons:
There is a good selection of weapons in the game, but the real issue is with practicality. Take, for instance, the so-called top sniper rifle in the game - the Kraber. It's supposed to be a .50-cal sniper rifle. It LOOKS great, but that's where the good news ends. If you hop into the firing range and test out all of the sniper rifles available to you, you will catch the glaring issues. The Sentinel, the Longbow, and the Charge Rifle all use sniper rounds (NOT a .50; Something smaller like a .308). All three can reach WAY out and touch your enemy. The Charge Rifle can literally reach all the way across an area of the map - over 800m. The Sentinel and Longbow can shoot pretty accurately to 400+m (depends on optics in use, graphics, screen size, FOV, etc). With the Kraber, the bullet starts dropping wildly at just 200m. Yeah...the highest-powered weapon in the game, using the highest-caliber bullet can BARELY eke out a 400m hit with accuracy. Let's add to this the 30-30 Repeater and the G7 Scout - A heavy ammo, medium range pew-pew and light ammo medium range pew-pew, respectively. Both of these rifles can out-shoot the Kraber with accuracy. WHY? And the Charge Rifle - Why does this not use energy ammo? I mean...CHARGE Rifle...it shoots a beam of light!...sigh...

5. Legends:
Don't get me wrong, there is a use for every single legend in the game. Whether it be for hiding, sniping, guarding, tracking...it's useful stuff. It is also getting really out of hand. First, how many freaking legends does a game like this need? At some point in the near future, you could probably have a pub match where every single player in the game is a different legend. I'm not even joking though I wish I were. Second, when EA unveils a new legend, they typically add it to the game and then they forget its existence. No re-balancing of legends, no fixing bugs, etc. And if they DO fix something with a legend, it is usually a heavy-handed nerf beyond what anyone that actually PLAYS the game was expecting. The abilities of the legends are pretty unique, but the overall effect of those abilities is copied across other legends. The exception to this is both Loba and Lifeline. Loba has her black market (so you don't have to hunt around an area if you know what you are looking for) and Lifeline has her health drone - The only legend that can heal your flesh-wounds. Other than those two, you can pretty much classify all other legends into categories like defense, offense, or recon and their abilities, while varied, have ultimately the same effect on the game. Offense legends can quickly get up in your face and kill you, defense legends can slow your entry into an area while sapping your health, and recon legends can track you and your team down. Simple. And boring too. Meh.

On to my ideas on how we can fix BOTH the cheater AND MM issues in Apex:

1. New DB table - Player AVG DMG (>10) Last 10 Games (PAD).

2. New DB table - Player AVG DMG Rating (PADR); 11-300: Rating 0; 301-700: Rating 1; 701-1200: Rating 2; 1201-2000: Rating 3; 2001-3200: Rating 4; 3201-4200: Rating 5 (AND account marked for review); 4200+: Rating 6 (Insta-banned - If the pros can't do it, pubs can't either without cheating).

*NOTE - Keep in mind that these are averaged over the last TEN games where damage done was greater than 10.

3. Players can only be matched with other players of the same PADR -/+1.

4. Teams have an AVG DMG Rating (TADR) of ((PADR1+PADR2+PADR3)/3)-1 (always rounded UP) for BR Trios. 1 player with R2, 2 players with R3 would be ((R2+R3+R3)/3)-1=R2. Teams can only be matched with other teams of the same TADR.

THREE birds, one stone. Fix MM, catch a boatload of cheaters, AND the games are more fun because you are playing with players very close to your own skill level instead of non-stop sweats OR non-stop noobs.

*I'm not saying it is not possible to play a 4K+ DMG game. I AM saying it IS impossible to play 10 *consecutive* 4K+ DMG games without cheating. Again, if the pros can't do it, neither can the pubs without programmatic assistance (cheating).

Elden Ring is an experience unlike anything I’ve played before. FromSoftware took the best elements of its previous Soulsborne games and seamlessly brought them together in a vast, interconnected open world. It feels like the culmination of everything the studio has learned and perfected over the past decade. The first impression of Limgrave is outstanding. The atmosphere is breathtaking, the landscapes are stunning, and the sheer sense of scale and mystery immediately draws you into the world. Every corner of the map holds something new to discover, whether it’s a hidden cave, an ancient ruin, or an unexpected boss encounter. The world constantly rewards curiosity and makes exploration feel genuinely exciting. You never quite know what awaits you beyond the next hill and that sense of discovery is what makes the experience so special.

The combat is equally outstanding. It feels smooth, challenging, and incredibly rewarding. The boss fights are another major highlight, offering a huge variety of enemies and memorable battles that constantly challenge you to adapt. The variety of weapons, spells, and abilities allows you to experiment with different builds and find your own approach to almost every encounter. What truly elevates Elden Ring, however, is how its systems work together. The items you discover can fundamentally change how you approach the game. This variety also gives Elden Ring exceptional replayability. A second playthrough can feel like a completely different adventure simply because you choose another build, discover areas you missed the first time or approach familiar encounters with a new perspective. The world is so densely packed with content that completing the main story is only one part of what the game has to offer. 

And then there is the Shadow of the Erdtree expansion, which is absolutely worth experiencing. It builds upon the strengths of the base game with new environments, challenging enemies, memorable boss encounters, and an impressive amount of additional content. The difficulty can be demanding, but that is part of what makes the experience so rewarding. Rather than feeling like an unnecessary addition, the expansion feels like a substantial continuation of the adventure and further demonstrates FromSoftware's ability to create compelling worlds filled with secrets and challenges.

What makes all of this especially meaningful to me is how rarely a game manages to leave such a lasting impression. The last time I felt this much joy and love for a game was around 15 years ago with Elder Scrolls Skyrim. Both games capture that feeling of stepping into a new world and wanting to explore every corner of it. For me, it is one of the most memorable gaming experiences in recent years and a genuine masterpiece of the open-world RPG genre. Everything Elden Ring has to offer makes it an incredible gaming experience. If you enjoy immersive worlds, rewarding combat, meaningful exploration, and the freedom to shape your own adventure, I cannot recommend Elden Ring highly enough. It’s been a long time since a game resonated with me this much. I genuinely wish I could experience it all over again for the first time. I highly recommend playing it!

Elden Ring is an incredible game that offers an unforgettable adventure. The world is massive, beautiful and full of secrets, with countless places to explore, hidden bosses to discover and weapons to experiment with.

One of its biggest strengths is the freedom it gives you. The build variety is fantastic, and experimenting with different weapons, spells and playstyles makes every run feel unique. The boss fights, lore and atmosphere are also outstanding, and the sense of discovery when you stumble upon something completely unexpected is hard to beat.

My only real criticism is that the open world can sometimes feel too big and exhausting. After a while, exploring every corner starts to feel more like a checklist than an adventure. And while the PvE experience is exceptional, the invasions and PvP never really clicked with me as much as I hoped.

Still, I completed 100% and absolutely loved the journey. Despite a few flaws, Elden Ring is a monumental achievement and a game every action RPG fan should experience.

Elden Ring is a good game, but it's so bogged down by its own weight that I don't think I've ever encountered a game that's overstayed its welcome to this degree. 

Prior to playing, I'd read the criticisms of reused content and open world recycling, but I genuinely didn't think it would be as bad as it actually is. You know that meme, where it's [Game] (picture of things clustered together) and [Open World Game] (picture of same things spaced apart)? I don't think that actually captures the dynamic of Elden Ring. That sentiment implies that an open-world game has bespoke, quality content with stretches of empty space between them. In reality, the situation is actually worse in Elden Ring. It's not that there's quality content separated by empty space -- it's actually mediocre content separated by empty space.

So, so, SO much of the content in Elden Ring simply isn't worth doing, at all. Your first Catacomb is worth doing for novelty, sure, but the fifth and tenth one certainly aren't. You will find the same exact enemy types and design principles in every single one -- by having experienced one Catacomb, you have experienced them all (and the first experience, frankly, isn't particularly memorable anyhow). Sadly, Catacombs are actually one of the more interesting POI types in Elden Ring, since they tend to have more involved  layouts and traps. Other POI types, like Caves, are abysmally boring, being indistinct, featureless tunnels, and some, like Ruins, barely qualify as content at all, being literally a staircase into a chest and nothing more. To add insult to injury, rewards are infrequently worth your time, often being a consumable material you have dozens of and a spirit ash no human in history has ever actually equipped to their hotbar. These two things, in tandem, mean that exploring POIs in Elden Ring have neither intrinsic nor extrinsic value -- you don't want to do them for their own sake, and you don't want to do them for the item rewards, either.

The result of this dynamic is that nothing in Elden Ring really feels new past the first area. In them, the majority of things to find are the same stale, bland POIs you've already experienced. Liurnia might as well be Blue Limgrave, Caelid be Red Limgrave, Altus Yellow Limgrave, and so on. While they might be "new" areas, they house the same tired content you've already experienced prior to entering them. In that way, the entire world collapses. Reuse is the name of the game: POIs, enemies, bosses, field enemies. I found myself actively skipping most field content past the 40-50 hour mark. Why make a 80-100 hour game, then, if much of it isn't worth playing? It calls into question the entire open-world format; it's structurally flawed, and Elden Ring is no exception. You have functionally experienced 80% of the gameplay loop by the time you have cleared the Weeping Peninsula.

What about the other 20%, then? Well, the other 20% is some of the best content in video gaming, ever. The legacy dungeons -- the actual quality, bespoke content one might hope to see in a video game -- are truly exceptional. Areas like Leyndell and Nokstella will simply astonish you with their atmosphere, layout, and exploration. These zones are exceptional, and the usual Soulslike successes -- weighty combat, tense experience loss mechanics -- shine as you make your way through these imaginative and exhilarating zones. They evoke fantastical wonder and white-knuckle adrenaline in equal measure.

Legacy dungeons are truly a joy to play through, but they beg the obvious question: why weren't these the whole game? Why did Fromsoft waste so much time on ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Cave #20-30 instead of just developing actually good content? Elden Ring feels open world for the sake of being open world -- the structure adds very little, if anything, to the game but takes so much. The opportunity cost of developing at scale is too steep to ameliorate, even for veteran developers with the resources and creative freedom to execute their vision somewhat faithfully. I understand that there's a sense of epicness that comes with a sheer size, but I don't think it was worth it for Elden Ring. The game would be twice as good if it were half the size, filled with content that's actually worth doing. I understand the desire to break away from the Dark Souls brand, but, in my opinion, nothing about the trade was worth it -- especially so since the best parts of the game (like interwoven dungeon layouts, expanded character movesets, and weapon art customizability) are just Dark Souls+.

Ultimately, I do recommend Elden Ring, but with the heavy caveat that it is the victim of its own ambition. The game is too big, too empty, too formulaic for its own good. I do understand why Elden Ring is beloved, and I do understand why it's such a seminal title in gaming. I'll also admit that I've never particularly cared for the open-world format. But I truly believe that, subjective opinions aside, it does more harm than good to Elden Ring. I've played for about 80 hours, enjoyed much of it, and am very near the end of the game, but I simply don't have the stamina to continue. Maybe I'll pick it up again in the future, but the friction is grinding.

There's enjoyment to be had, but be warned: you have a lot of chores to do between the fun.

Elden Ring – A master...piece of ♥♥♥♥

Elden Ring is a weird game. Beautiful graphics, fantastic combat, incredible world design, yet I spent much of my playthrough wondering whether I was having fun.
The world is full of memorable places, classic FromSoftware gameplay, and some genuinely fun enemies and bosses.
And then there's Torrent. The horse. The legend. The actual secret weapon. Forget legendary swords. Running past 90% of the nonsense is probably the most useful ability in the game.

Elden Ring has two gameplay modes: explore endlessly or git gud.

Exploration becomes exhausting. The world is enormous, yet regular enemies are barely a threat. You spend hours checking every cliff and cave, collecting hundreds of items you'll never use.
Another cookbook? Fantastic. Another crafting material? Just what I needed.
The game makes you explore every edge of the map because maybe something useful is hidden there. Spoiler: usually there isn't. Or it's not what you need.

Then there's the difficulty balance.

Without Mimic Tear, some bosses feel like beating a brick wall with a toothpick. With Mimic Tear, suddenly you're the brick wall. There's little middle ground between getting destroyed and watching your clone do half the work.
I love challenging combat, but I'd rather feel I won than found the unofficial easy-mode switch. 

And finally, the story.

Cryptic lore, depressing characters, dying worlds, NPCs speaking in riddles. Classic FromSoftware. But Elden Ring feels particularly bleak. I never felt like a hero.
The Chosen Undead in DS1 and Ashen One in DS3 weren't traditional heroes either. These games are about struggling through broken worlds. But Elden Ring gave me little reason to care about becoming Elden Lord.

The verdict?

Brilliant ideas, fantastic combat, breathtaking environments, memorable moments.
Also bloated, repetitive, frustrating, and obsessed with rewarding exploration with stuff nobody needs.
When it's good, it's brilliant. When it's bad, you're riding Torrent around another cliff looking for an item you'll never use.

A game I can admire more easily than I can love.

A 10,000-line review will not fit in one response. I can write it in numbered parts, keeping the review overwhelmingly positive and avoiding repetition.

Elden Ring: A Monumental Triumph of Open-World Design

Elden Ring is not merely a successful action role-playing game. It is a vast, mysterious, and deeply rewarding adventure that demonstrates what an open world can achieve when discovery matters more than checklists. FromSoftware takes the demanding combat, intricate environments, and cryptic storytelling associated with its earlier games and expands them across the Lands Between without sacrificing their identity.

The opening hours establish the game's confidence immediately. After a brief introduction, the player emerges into Limgrave and sees a landscape filled with ruins, forests, cliffs, castles, and distant landmarks. The game does not overwhelm the screen with icons or insist upon a rigid itinerary. Instead, it invites curiosity. A ruined church may contain a merchant. A forest might conceal an underground elevator. A distant tower could become the beginning of an adventure lasting several hours.

This approach makes exploration feel personal. Players are not simply clearing activities selected from a menu; they are constructing their own journeys. One person may travel directly toward Stormveil Castle, while another spends hours investigating caves, fighting optional bosses, gathering equipment, and discovering characters in unexpected locations. Both experiences feel valid because the world accommodates different priorities without losing its carefully designed structure.

The Lands Between is enormous, but its scale is supported by remarkable environmental variety. Limgrave's green plains create a welcoming yet melancholy beginning. Liurnia of the Lakes surrounds the player with mist, flooded ruins, and magical institutions. Caelid presents a diseased landscape whose crimson skies and grotesque creatures communicate danger before a single enemy attacks. Later territories continue to introduce distinctive architecture, weather, terrain, and atmosphere.

These regions are visually memorable because they do more than change the scenery. Each area produces a different emotional response. Limgrave encourages adventurous confidence. Caelid inspires dread. Leyndell creates awe through its immense golden architecture and layered streets. The Mountaintops of the Giants convey isolation through snow, wind, and tremendous empty spaces. The environments serve as storytelling devices, shaping the player's understanding of a fractured world.

Torrent, the player's spectral steed, makes this immense landscape pleasurable to traverse. Torrent moves quickly, can double-jump, and gives exploration a sense of freedom. The mount allows players to leap over obstacles, climb unconventional routes, and escape dangerous encounters. Mounted combat adds another dimension, particularly when fighting dragons or groups of enemies across open fields.

The absence of excessive guidance is one of the game's greatest strengths. Elden Ring trusts players to observe their surroundings. Statues can point toward hidden catacombs. Unusual rock formations may indicate concealed paths. A distant structure can become a navigational reference. Even the fragments required to reveal each portion of the map must be found in the world, turning cartography into part of the adventure.

The map itself is beautifully designed. Rather than functioning as a sterile interface, it resembles an illustrated artifact filled with geographical clues. Drawn ruins, mines, forests, and unusual formations encourage investigation. A careful player can often predict where something interesting might be located without the game explicitly identifying it. This preserves mystery while rewarding attention.

Combat remains the foundation of the experience. Every encounter asks the player to consider distance, timing, stamina, positioning, and enemy behaviour. Attacks have weight, shields provide meaningful protection, and dodges demand judgment. Victory rarely comes from pressing buttons thoughtlessly. Even ordinary opponents can punish carelessness, which makes successful encounters satisfying.

The game's difficulty is demanding, but it is unusually flexible. Players can improve their attributes, upgrade weapons, summon spirits, use cooperative multiplayer, exploit elemental weaknesses, or leave a difficult area and return later. These options do not trivialise the adventure. They create multiple ways to overcome its challenges and allow a broader range of players to find a workable strategy.

Build diversity is exceptional. A character can become a heavily armoured knight, a swift duelist, a destructive sorcerer, a faithful healer, an archer, or a warrior who combines several disciplines. The enormous selection of weapons, spells, shields, talismans, armour sets, and consumable items encourages experimentation. Discovering a new piece of equipment can inspire an entirely different style of play.

Weapons feel distinct rather than interchangeable. Colossal swords strike slowly but deliver tremendous impact. Spears control space and allow cautious attacks. Curved swords reward aggression and mobility. Bows offer ranged utility, while magical staffs and sacred seals open extensive spell systems. Even weapons within the same category may possess different attack patterns, scaling properties, or special abilities.

The Ashes of War system deepens this variety. These abilities can grant weapons dramatic techniques, from powerful leaps and spinning attacks to magical projectiles and defensive manoeuvres. Many Ashes of War also allow players to modify a weapon's affinity, helping it complement a chosen distribution of attributes. The system makes ordinary equipment adaptable and gives experimentation practical value.

Magic is particularly impressive. Sorceries and incantations are not limited to variations of basic projectiles. Players can summon spectral weapons, manipulate gravity, breathe like dragons, hurl lightning, conjure flames, cure ailments, strengthen allies, and unleash enormous beams of magical energy. The visual spectacle supports a system with genuine tactical breadth.

Spirit Ashes are another valuable addition. These summonable companions range from packs of wolves to powerful individual warriors. They can distract bosses, apply status effects, or contribute substantial damage. More importantly, they let players shape the rhythm of difficult battles. A fight that feels overwhelming alone can become manageable when a spirit divides the enemy's attention.

The bosses are among the game's defining achievements. Major opponents combine imaginative visual design, memorable music, elaborate arenas, and complex attack patterns. Their movements often communicate personality: some fight with disciplined precision, others with animalistic violence, and others with supernatural grandeur. Learning these encounters can initially feel intimidating, but improvement is tangible.

Margit provides an excellent early lesson. His delayed attacks punish panic, his quick follow-ups test positioning, and his aggression forces players to engage with the combat system. Defeating him feels meaningful because the battle teaches patience rather than merely checking numerical strength. It establishes that observation and adaptation will be essential throughout the journey.

Godrick is equally memorable for different reasons. His grotesque appearance embodies the game's themes of ambition, decay, and stolen power. The encounter escalates spectacularly, combining brutal axe attacks with a transformation that is both horrifying and absurdly magnificent. It is a perfect example of FromSoftware's ability to unite mechanical challenge with unforgettable imagery.

Rennala's battle demonstrates the game's theatrical range. Its dreamlike staging, magical effects, and haunting atmosphere distinguish it from conventional duels.

It is a hard game.  That's fine by itself, but there are multiple ways a game can be hard.  This game is hard in some legitimate ways, but also is hard and/or tedious in ways that just plain suck.

The camera can easily get occluded indoors and you are fighting blind.  In a souls game that kills you.

The lock on handling with "nimble" opponents will cause your movement to become extremely unpredictable, forcing you to constantly lock/unlock.  Meanwhile, locking is very clunky, sometimes locking something in the next room or just snapping your camera to forward which makes it even harder to regain the lock and, again, this kills you in a souls game.

Affordance is terrible.  Fans call this a feature (i.e. you don't know what level stuff is, etc.).  It would be if you could judge opponents in any way other than facetanking and dying.  You'll end up with giants you slay easily, then that small mob with a reused skin you recall from the lowbie area spanks you.  When minibosses beat you, you have no idea when you should come back.  As a result, the vast majority of what would be fun/challenging encounters are either - (a) you die, leave and maybe come back later or (b) oh yeah, let me go back there and... oh I killed it easily because I'm 20 levels higher now.

Also on a similar note, the game doesn't explain extremely important topics like leveling a weapon is more important than stats.  Or when a weapon scales with some attribute as "B" or "D", what does that even mean?

You find a boss and it barely takes damage.  Is it resistant to your damage type or are you just not high enough level?  Who knows!  Hey let's sink a ton of smithing stones into a blunt weapon just to find out and I sure hope I didn't just waste them.

Poor affordance and esoteric drops basically gating progression gives you two choices in the game: spend 10s of hours banging your head against the game to figure out the special place you need to go, to kill the miniboss, to get a drop you didn't know it had, to then give the drop to another NPC on the other side of the map, which will cause them to then sell you Smithing Stone[2] so you don't have to spend 20 hours farming Limgrave mines with a drop rate so low you aren't even sure it drops there..... OR you go to YouTube, find the cheese/needed steps and you're done in 30 minutes.

While on YouTube, you then notice some "great start to ER" videos and you watch one.  It shows you how to run around picking up all the somber smithing stones, open tons of chests and finally cheese a dragon so you have an incredibly powerful character.  All with zero real combat.  But yeah, Elden Ring is "hard" and you need to "git gud" and totally not a poorly crafted unbalanced and clunky mess of a game.

I will probably beat it in anger.  But if you don't own it, don't buy it.

Cyberpunk 2077 is nothing short of a monumental achievement in modern gaming. Its meticulously crafted open world, breathtaking visual fidelity, and extraordinarily immersive atmosphere set a benchmark that few titles can even aspire to reach. Night City is not merely a backdrop for the narrative; it is a living, breathing metropolis, teeming with moral ambiguity, social stratification, technological obsession, and the haunting consequences of unchecked corporate power.

What truly distinguishes the game, however, is its narrative sophistication. Beneath its dazzling neon lights and futuristic spectacle lies a profoundly human story about identity, mortality, freedom, and the desperate pursuit of meaning in an increasingly dehumanised world. Its characters are remarkably nuanced, its dialogue often incisive, and its most emotionally resonant moments linger long after the credits roll.

Visually, Cyberpunk 2077 is nothing less than extraordinary. The interplay of neon illumination, atmospheric fog, intricate environmental detail, and sophisticated lighting techniques creates an aesthetic that is simultaneously mesmerising and unsettling. Night City feels as though it has been ripped from the darkest, most compelling visions of the future and brought to life with astonishing technical precision.

Ultimately, Cyberpunk 2077 transcends the boundaries of conventional entertainment. It is an ambitious, thought-provoking, and occasionally heartbreaking exploration of what it means to remain human in a world that increasingly treats humanity as a commodity. Few games manage to combine such artistic ambition, narrative depth, and technological brilliance so convincingly. Cyberpunk 2077 is not merely a game worth experiencing; it is an experience that exemplifies the extraordinary artistic potential of the medium itself.

i love that v actually says what you chose. it's a small thing, but to chose no, and have v actually say "no way hose" feels really immersive. so many games just have npcs just talk at you and you never actually reply. of course, i understand that it's a lot of work to make voice lines for every single thing you say, but i think cyberpunk is a perfect example that it is worth it. 

the world feels real, and the characters feel rounded and diverse. no one is perfect, and people make questionable choices that backfire.

After over 600 hours in this game, I can safely say, this game is really overrated. Nothing you choose or do in the game matters. Murder a bunch of Valentinos? They treat you just the same, and Padre wouldn't even bat an eye. Have 5 star police wanted levels? No problem, enter a save zone, in and out and the all the police simultaneously suffers from collective amnesia. The dialogue choice barely matters either, why give me the choice if it doesn't matter? All you're doing is wasting my time making a choice that does nothing. 

And it's not just the lackluster RPG mechanics. The writing in this game is also aggressively mid. The game want us to treat Jackie like an old friend, and want us to feel sad when he dies, but barely give us much time to get to know him personally, how am I supposed to feel for a character that I barely know? Your character V also doesn't have much agencies within the narrative, and by extension a character arc. Not even 1 hour in Johnny immediately hijacks the story and the rest of the story is basically V being taken along for the ride in Johnny's story, hell one of the endings are literally just johnny taking over at the end and V not even being aware of what's going on. V themself also is a very selfish and shallow character, what else does V wanted out of their life other than becoming a legend, get rich, or survive; I really can't find anything else that V values even towards the end. The game does not give me a reason to root for V, and there is also no sense of urgency to V's condition beyond the cutscenes, I just doesn't care about V at all as a character, let alone engage with their story. 

The world building is also extremely generic. Hell it's name literally is just it's genre + 2077, you could not find a game that is more of a parody of cyberpunk than this game. "Oh no! AI will take over!" Yeah like I haven't seen this story already in Terminator, 2001 a Space Odyssey, The Matrix, I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream, Dune, exc... all of them have a deeper exploration into the topic than this game does. And the concept of Rogue AI is also so dumb, like the writer don't understand how technology works, they think AI programs can just "exist" in the magical realm that is the net, without requiring a hardware to run on, like human's can't just locate the server that contains the rogue AI and cut it's power source. And don't even get me started on "Capitalism Bad" and how even more generic and milked to death that topic is. Night City also don't give my any desire to explore it, when basically 95% of the building is just a shell with no interiors, filled with pedestrians that are dumber than a squirrel. Fallout 4 gives me better motivation to explore it's world than this game, and it's literally just a wasteland. There just isn't anything interesting in night city to explore and discover, most of the lore are basically shards with text messages for me to read telling the same generic miserable story about, you guess it, "Capitalism Bad". There is also very little philosophical exploration on the nature of identity, in a game where the story is literally about one person's identity overriding the other, which is just another massive waste of potential in a mountain of wasted potential that is this game. Like imagine V contemplating what it means to be yourself, and questioning rather or not merging with another person's identity is really that bad, like what if instead of Johnny taking over, their identity merges and becomes a whole new person that is neither Johnny or V, imagine the potential of the premise of transferable consciousness and identity, but NO, this game doesn't explore ANY of those possibilities! Ghost in the Shell explore a lot of these topics, so I don't know why they didn't even study one of the most popular cyberpunk franchise out there and learn from it, like I'm not even asking you to have original ideas, at least match the depth of other stories in the same genre! 

I can use two words to summarize this game: Wasted Potential. Choices don't matter, characters don't develop, generic world building, shallow narrative, and I haven't even mention all the unfulfilled promises that they still haven't remotely fulfilled. This game is just too overrated for me to recommend it.

What a ride. The worldbuilding in Cyberpunk is great—it immediately sets the tone for the world you will soon be let loose in, showing the rawness and dystopian nature of Night City. The game covers a lot of subjects, such as politics, the economy, corporations, history, the loss of a loved one, depression, PTSD, and more.

I initially dropped this game somewhere around the end of Act I and returned months later. I decided to start a completely fresh playthrough since I had forgotten a lot of the story. It wasn't until this playthrough that I got the opportunity to appreciate how dynamic the gameplay can be. The Skill Tree allows for a plethora of choices on how YOU want to play Cyberpunk 2077. Want to be a Cyberpsycho with a katana and a Sandy (Sandevistan) to slow down time? Sure. Prefer to be a brute with Gorilla Arms and land explosive punches? Go ahead. Want to be a Skyrim-like stealth archer, but with a silenced pistol? It's here. The gameplay really is GREAT!

I wasn't here when the game was the infamous dumpster fire we all know. But I can testify the game is great now and runs smoothly, especially on a mid-tier setup like mine (specs attached). Easily getting 130-160 FPS.

However, there's something that bugs me, and it's the story pacing. Act I is phenomenal. It introduces the main character, their backstory of your choice, the heist, and [spoiler] Johnny Silverhand—showing the consequences of raw ambition for fame, glory, and riches. [/spoiler]

Personally, the game carries the story well... until the end of Act II. Suddenly, everything just feels very rushed and lackluster once you reach the Point of No Return. I also found, disappointingly, Act III to be extremely short in comparison to the others. I played multiple endings and found most of them just... meh? Like, c'mon. The game kicks off with a bang... literally. But towards the end, it feels like a slow-burning candle with an almost exhausted wick.

Aside from that, I really have nothing negative to say about Cyberpunk 2077. The creativity that went into this is WILD. Props to CD Projekt Red for not doing an Anthem and instead standing behind this project.

I think it's both easy and difficult to describe just how good of a game Cyberpunk 2077 turned out to be from the way I experienced it. In one sentence, Cyberpunk 2077 is probably one of the most well-made, wholeheartedly complete games that exists out there. The entire world of Cyberpunk basically lived by its code of making a name for yourself that it itself spawned a majorly successful anime, collaborations, comics and books, a whole new fandom out of it. Just the CD Projekt effect maybe. 

Else, Cyberpunk 2077 certainly has some flaws that to others may have been the arrow to the knee for them, but I'm going to be describing how I felt. And in spite of the minor flaws it had, as a whole, I felt very, VERY content with it all. 

I spent the past year and a bit playing this game, on and off, taking breaks that were months long before picking it up again, and every time I did, I got right back into the groove of completely absorbing myself into the world of Night City like I never left. Some games when I've played after a certain time away from it, I end up struggling to reconnect. But with Cyberpunk, it never felt like that at all. 

Every character actually had depth. I sympathised with more than one character and wanted to learn of their back stories more than ever. Learning characters back stories? Who would've thought. The side gigs - sure, some of them got repetitive - but they at least were different in that each gig occasionally had motives. They had clues, evidence of something else going on, and at some point Cyberpunk 2077 the action RPG turned into a mystery thriller game. The combat is extremely versatile. I mostly played a Netrunner build for my V with quickhacks and non-confrontational attacks, but when I restarted and decided to go for a mostly Mercenary frontal assault V, it was just as smooth of a transition to be a ruthless killer slicing enemies with katanas and shooting everybody down with the spray of your machine gun. 

I finished the whole game, completed all gigs, got all tarots, played the DLC with all endings through and through, and I can say without a doubt that I'll be remembering Cyberpunk 2077 for a long time. In fact, I know that once I finish this review to go to uninstall this game, I'm actually going to miss it. I intend to keep it as one of my most favourite games of all time for the kind of impact it has on my experience as a gamer towards video games, and if anything, I hope that when people pick this game up or wonder if this game was the right choice to start playing, they haven't seen anything yet.

There are a LOT of ways to customize your character, from weapons, to skills, to clothes, and to cyberware, and you can really create some interesting combinations. Plus, there is so much leveling! Normal leveling, plus skill progression, plus street cred! By the end of the game, I'm a powerhouse with armor, health, weapon damage, and resistances, mowing my way through whatever crosses my path.

The main issue is the story SUCKSSSSSSSS. There are fun and interesting parts of the story, but a lot of it is slow and unskippable. I've done the main story all the way through twice, and there are so many dead moments. There is also a lot of slow walking behind someone, sometimes while they explain something you can't skip. There are a lot of times where you have to [spoiler]fight as Johnny, removing any and all upgrades/cyberware/weapons you've gotten but keeping the level difficulty. You get thrown into a completely new playstyle at a high level with no way to manual save! It's the only part of the game I really die in.[/spoiler]

Plus, [spoiler]I love Keanu Reeves, but Johnny is ANNOYING. And your relationship is applied inconsistently. Why am I being forced to say I hate him when I spent the entire game building rapport? Why am I forced to say I like him around when we have no relationship to speak of? There are times where he tells you to do something, and if you don't do it, you're treated like an idiot by the game, and there are times where you are treated like an idiot if you DO listen to him. It's all very confusing and jarring. [/spoiler]

Speaking of characters, Judy and Panam are fine, but the male romance options are TERRIBLE. You have a [spoiler]corrupt cop who tries to play puppy after dragging you through corrupt cop ♥♥♥♥[/spoiler] and then you have [spoiler]the 80 year old rockstar who is still in love with the man in your head who tries to destroy three girls careers because he's a bitter washed up ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.[/spoiler] Plus, both male romance options are side quest locked, so completely missable, while Judy and Panam are met through the main plot.

Heck, even Judy has her problems. Judy [spoiler]is left sad in all endings except one that has nothing to do with her. Why am I becoming distant and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ to her in the mansion ending? My V wouldn't do that?[/spoiler] I haven't finished the Panam romance yet, but it's... weird so far too.

Also, the gigs. There are so many gigs with secret requirements that aren't communicated in anyway. Sometimes it will say "Don't be seen (optional)" but a LOT of times, the game expects you to be stealthy or not kill people or whatever and you only find out at the end of the mission when the fixer is disappointed in you. It happened with EVERY fixer, to the point that I dropped a save before EVERY gig so I could go back and do it again in case of secret expectations.

The biggest sin of the story has got to be the extreme cynicism. By the time I was getting to the end of the game, I knew that if I was going out of my way to save someone, there was a pretty high chance they would [spoiler]kill themselves.[/spoiler] It literally just kept happening. There are so many times where you try so hard to do good things, and it almost feels like the game is laughing at you for trying. I actually really like grimdark, gritty, and cynical media, but this was almost unpalatable in some cases because instead of "everything is literally as bad as possible, but you can do something" it very much has the feeling of "everything is bad and you're stupid for thinking you could make ANYTHING better." There are a couple places where you can do something, but it's mostly punished in my experience.

All this to say, the story is frustrating and mean and painful. There isn't a single ending [spoiler]where you don't die,[/spoiler] which has some foreshadowing, but it really feels like the last f u to [spoiler]give you hope and then show you that it's hopeless.[/spoiler]

The reason I have 184 hours (and why I will almost certainly have more) is that the gameplay is genuinely so fun. I feel like I can recommend this game, despite all the huge issues, because you can literally just not play the story. I have a character right now that I started with phantom liberty, but instead of doing the DLC, I just ran around and did all the NCPD side quests and killed enemies wherever they showed up. That it the real fun of the game. Running around the map with your cool abilities and awesome guns and mindlessly killing stuff to level up. I could, and have, done it for hours, and it's something I've even used to relax.

I would say get this game on sale and be prepared for the slog to get to the good stuff, if you are willing. If you aren't willing to wade through everything above for a fun, brainless, in game murder spree, I don't recommend this game.

From the moment you step into Night City, the game pulls you into a beautifully constructed dystopian world. The overarching narrative unfolds gradually, paired with deep, immersive worldbuilding that makes the city feel alive and keeps you coming back for more. What sets it apart, though, is the emotional connection you form with the characters - every decision and conversation feels heavy, meaningful, and grounded. Throughout the entire gameplay loop, you never feel like you are completing filler content just for the sake of checking off a box; every mission carries real narrative weight.

Then comes Phantom Liberty—the ultimate cherry on top. Easily ranking among the best expansion packs ever created, it kicks off with a bang and maintains non-stop momentum straight through to the end.

Seeing where Cyberpunk 2077 started compared to where it sits today is nothing short of incredible. CDPR delivered a legendary gameplay experience, and getting to step into the shoes of V is an journey no RPG fan should miss

This game has a lot of content and it took me a long time to beat.  When I say "beat," I mean "perfect."  Because the only way to really beat the game is to 100% it, which is very time-consuming.

There's not really much of a story except for at the beginning.  Otherwise, you basically just build up your life, family, friends and town.  There are really only two mutually exclusive choices to make, but they mostly lead to similar outcomes, and the rewards are different.

When starting the game, you can choose what kind of farm you want between a regular farm, beach farm, a forage farm, a farm with monsters, etc.  The goal is still the same; sow, harvest, get paid.

I lost track of how many quests there were, mostly because a lot of them repeat.  If I were to summarize it into different parts, I'd limit it to the following:  Farming, mining, relationships and community.

Farming is what you would think; grow crops, build coops and stables, care for animals, produce artisan goods, craft stuff, cook dishes, etc.

Mining is more of the adventurous and combative part of the game where you explore the floors of mines, fight enemies, find rare resources and artifacts, forge, find and upgrade weapons, etc.

Relationships involve the local and non-local citizens.  Talking to them, gifting them things they like or completing quests for them increase your relationship.  In contrast, saying mean things, hitting trashcans in front of them, or gifting them things they don't like will decrease your relationship.  There are events that happen at various times and places once you've reached a certain relationship threshold with a particular person and it reveals a little more depth to their lives and develops their character further.  There are bachelors and bachelorettes that can be romanced and eventually married, after which they move in with you, enabling you to have/adopt up to 2 children.  Some of this cannot be done until you've upgraded your house sufficiently.  There are a number of characters that are either already married or cannot otherwise be romanced.  There are mods that can change this, FYI.  I didn't use any of them, for the record.

The community-related part of the game involves developments that improve things around town, like fixing buses, boats or bridges that lead to new places, fixing the greenhouse on your property for indoor farming, removing rocks so that ore and minerals flow through the town's water, etc.  This is the part where there are two mutually exclusive ways to go about it.  The developer has made it very apparent that one of these ways is their preferred way, and is a lot more in-depth and time-consuming in nature.  The other way is more efficient, but is made to feel more empty in the end.  Some of the new places revealed by these developments are beyond the local town, and there are different caves, mines, farms, people and quests to work with.  Like I said, this game has a lot of content.

I can see why so many people like this game.  I'd say the unfortunate part for me was that I got overwhelmed at one point and had to put it down.  I came back a few years later to complete it.  It's difficult to do this, however, because I had to remember how everything worked and how I left things originally. 

Anyway, I think most adventure gamers, or people who like games such as Terraria or Minecraft would enjoy this game a lot.

Feels silly to leave a review on a game so well known as this, but gotta let CA know I appreciate his attitude towards fans. 

Lots of replayability because you can decide if you want to prioritize money, friendships, or resources at the start of your run as well as farm layouts, marriage options, pets/farm animals, etc. 

It's no secret that a lot of us hate the fishing mechanic so it would be nice if there was an option to adjust it outside of rod and equipment purchases. However there is a way to get to level 5 fishing without fishing much or using mods.

Community Center Completion tip: [spoiler]I complete bundles the best I can/want to for easy rewards/farm help and then purchase the joja membership and pay to complete the remaining ones (it's the fish tank lets be honest). Membership fee is still the same but you only have to pay to complete bundles you haven't already completed so the overall cost is much less than if purchased from the beginning. It will no longer be a community center but a joja mart warehouse or whatever, so be sure to consider that. [/spoiler]

Mastering Fishing: [spoiler]Use the crab pots and just fish wherever it's easiest for you to do so. Better rods and bait/bobbers are available eventually to help further. The REAL way to quickly do this is read books. The fishing books help obviously BUT there are a handful of books that will send xp points to other skills if the main skill it's meant to benefit is maxed. I mastered fishing this way within 4years without prioritizing it. Bookseller and traveling cart merchant are where to go. [/spoiler]

Pretty much anything else can be modded and CA has always openly supported the mod community. I recommend playing without mods as long as possible to best understand the game as many popular mods add a lot of new content and it can be overwhelming for new players.
